title: Behavioral, new grad software engineer, strong answers

questions.text: Tell me about a project you owned from start to finish.
Tell me about a time you worked closely with someone who had a different working style.
Tell me about something that did not go to plan and what you learned.
Tell me about a disagreement in a team project.
Tell me about a time you explained something technical to a non-technical person.
Tell me about work you did that had a measurable effect on users.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Lena, thanks for joining. I'm Sam, an engineer on the platform team. This is a thirty minute behavioral conversation.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Sam, thanks for having me. I'm looking forward to it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How has your final semester been so far?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Busy but good. I'm finishing my capstone and teaching assistant work for the databases course.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Great. I'll ask about three or four past experiences, then leave time for your questions at the end.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a project you owned from start to finish.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: During my internship at Fernhill Payments I owned a tool that flagged duplicate refund requests. Support agents were catching duplicates by hand, about 40 a week. I wrote the design doc, got feedback from two senior engineers, built the matching job in Python, and added a review screen. I chose a simple rule on amount, card and a 48 hour window instead of a model, because we had no labeled data. After launch it caught 92 percent of duplicates in the first month and saved the support team about 6 hours a week.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What would you change if you built it again?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would talk to the agents earlier. I only met them in week three, and they told me partial refunds also counted as duplicates. That cost me a week of rework. Now I set up a user conversation in the first few days of any project.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a time you worked closely with someone who had a different working style.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: In my capstone, my partner liked to plan everything up front and I like to prototype. Early on we argued about whether to write the full API spec first. I suggested we each try our way for one day on separate endpoints and compare. His spec caught two naming problems my prototype missed, and my prototype found a slow query his spec did not. We agreed on a short spec plus a spike for anything risky, and we shipped all six milestones on time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about something that did not go to plan and what you learned.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: As a teaching assistant I wrote an autograder for a SQL assignment. I tested it only on my own solutions, and on the due date it failed 30 students whose queries were correct but ordered rows differently. I owned it in the course forum the same night, regraded everything by hand with one other assistant, and fixed the grader to compare sorted results. Since then I collect three or four real student answers before I trust any grader.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How do new graduates get their first project on your team?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Each new engineer gets a small, real project with a mentor in the first month, usually something that ships in four to six weeks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's all the time we have. Thanks Lena, the recruiter will follow up within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Sam. This was a good conversation.

notes: Strong for new grad: own role, numbers and a trade-off in each answer.
